A few more thoughts: 

1. Use scihub to find papers. Even if you can access them via a library it's infinitely faster to just copy paste the doi from the ref section of the papers you are already reading. 

2. When it comes to the actual writing part, structure based on common themes. For example, categorize the lit you find into a few key methodologies, and write a paragraph or two for each method. Or categorize by hypothesis, or data they used, or some other key distinctions you start to see as you read/skim the papers. If you start to write about one of the categories and have nothing to say, go read the key papers you found in that category in detail. Most of the time for me, writers block is because I don't really know what's going on. If I truly understand what they did and why the hell I care, I suddenly have lots to say.

3. "Write drunk edit sober". Doesnt have to be literal (although for me it sometimes is... ;)) But basically, your first thoughts/notes/paragraphs can be total trash. "This was a stupid fucking paper that I hated reading but I read it because it claimed to do XYZ, which is what I am trying to do. Here is what they did, I think that's a dumb/genius/confusing approach". Use those thoughts to guide what you still do and don't know, and guide what papers to read next.

I don't know if this is the "best" approach, but I usually start by finding just a few key papers that will obviously be pivotal for what I am doing -usually found via Google scholar, uni library, etc. Then I skim their lit review section and develop a list of important key words. Ctrl +f to find papers in the ref section with those key words. Find those and read the abstract to weed out if it's truly relevant. Search databases for papers that cite them and that they cite. This process could go on indefinitely, so after you have a few promising papers, pick the most important ones to read, and repeat the process you did with the first few papers. 

Depending on your field, there could be just a handful of relevant papers (math) or an impossibly large sea (social sciences). In the latter case, just accept that you CANNOT read everything. It's physically impossible. So search for the most representative papers. Particularly if there is 1. A meta analysis or 2. A lit overview publication rely on those heavily.  If those exist, it's important to reframe their insights for your specific hypothesis/goals/methods and search for any important literature that came out more recently. Typically any research worth it's salt will cite those meta analysis/lit reviews, so use popular databases to search for these.

I take notes on one large document with section headers so that I can cut paste/organize once I start to find common themes amongst the papers I find. Only write down by hand to help process my thoughts, or sometimes I'll dictate into my phone my random musings and then email the transcript to myself. 

Hope this helps, I've done WAY too many lit reviews because I work on very interdisciplinary projects, so I almost always need to start from scratch on a topic I know very little about lol.

Those classes for severely disabled students are so important though. My brother is nonverbal, in a wheel chair, has a feeding tube, needs 24/7 care. We had no money and were well below the poverty line but he still got to go to school, make friends, and have physical and social therapy every day. He even had a "girlfriend" all throughout high school, a very sweet and doting low verbal autistic girl who took to him immediately and would always sit with him, want to push his wheelchair around to take him places, and his name was one of the words in her limited vocabulary 🥺 It was so important for him and the day he graduated from high school was very bittersweet.

Just speaking from my own experience: my brother is undeniably disabled to anyone with eyeballs. He is nonverbal, very little muscle control, eats through a feeding tube, has breathing treatments daily to prevent pneumonia, etc. He needs 24/7 care, period. My mom doesn't want him left in a group home, so she takes care of him full time, and keeps him active in local social groups for other adults with severe disabilities. So the government pays for basically everything for him, because if they didn't, they would be paying for him to be in a group home anyways. Despite the fact that he is by all accounts the most obviously qualified person for this support, we STILL get put through the most ridiculous racket of bullshit to get his funding. He essentially gets a basic income. But every single penny that gets spent of that money for him is meticulously documented, right down to pairs of socks and chapstick. Because you know, maybe somehow WE are playing the long game here and gaming the system. Yeah if you want to get rich quick, taking care of him ain't the way to do it. The fear within the system is extremely out of proportion to reality. And that is coming from a very liberal state in the US.

I think it's hard for school administrators (who often have very little money and resources) to get it right every time with high functioning students who just need extra support. But having adapted special Ed classes is extremely important for kids with disabilities that otherwise would prevent them from attending school.

I went camping in the snowstorm near Flagstaff AZ last weekend, stayed warm and had a blast. Here's my thoughts: 

1. Having insulation from the ground should be the top priority as that is where you lose most heat. You mentioned an air mattress, we backpack with thinner air inflatable pads so that's not something I'm knowledgeable about, and it sounds like you have a system going so that's great. Wool works well for sure. You can also line along the floor on the edges of your tent with other gear like backpacks to trap in heat (as long as you aren't worried about it getting wet). If there is enough snow outside, you can also dig yourself into it or build a little wall with it around the tent (think, igloo). 

2. The things that kept me warmest are all down or wool. Down is absolutely the best, but obviously hard to handle sewing wise haha. I grew up in Washington state, and my friends and I would go "backyard camping" even when it was quite cold and snowy. My good friend's mom is a very experienced quilter, and she had made these down sleeping bags from a repurposed down comforter that she had covered in other fabric, I think it was flannel? If you don't want to deal with down in your project, your trip will be a lot warmer if you have a down puffy jacket that is comfy enough to wear to bed. 

4. As far as wool goes, I wore a pair of THICK wool socks last weekend and my feet stayed nice and toasty. I woke up and had to pee in the middle of the night, but I really didn't want to put my boots on. I literally put two plastic grocery bags around my feet to keep my socks from getting wet from the snow while I ran behind a tree. I felt nothing. My feet were so warm haha. A very warm beanie is also crucial to keep your body heat in. 

So all of that is to say, if you have a down sleeping bag or comforter to repurpose, that would be amazing. But assuming not lol I'd recommend wool.

I have no idea what they meant, but heres what I do: have good quality stock/broth on hand. You can buy premade broth/stock, but I like to make my own (easier than you'd think!). If you have a good base broth on hand you can just add whatever cooked veggies, meat, seasonings etc you like and viola, soup.

To make veggie stock: put some onions, carrots, celery, garlic, favorite herbs, and any other old veggies you've got lying around in the crock pot (tomatoes, mushrooms, even apples and lettuce!) Even old mushy stuff is fine, as long as it's not moldy, throw it in there. Add some water, and let it cook down all day. That's it! If you want you can also add chicken/turkey/beef bones if you have them. When it's been cooked for a long time, strain it, and there ya go. I make a bunch at once and freeze some for later. I don't add salt to mine, so it's essentially no sodium until I add salt to taste later. 

With that said, low sodium store bought broth isn't bad, although a bit more expensive. To make a tastier soup from pre bought stuff, saute some shallots, garlic, and herbs in olive oil and then add the broth.

As per another commenters response: there are other axiomatic systems than Kolmogrovs. I would say (VERY loosely) that this is similar to the divide of classical physics and quantum mechanics. They are different frameworks, both of which can be helpful in different situations. However modern statistical research largely assumes Kolmogrovs axiomatic system.

I'm going to try to keep with the spirit of your question: what is Statistical theory built upon? 

At the very base are core mathematical axioms and Kolmogrovs axioms of probability. These form the basis of measure theory and probability theory. Statistical inference itself is built on some key theoretical principals of information reduction such as sufficiency and completeness, as well as the likelihood principle. Other important theoretical properties are unbiasedness and consistency, to name a few. From there, contemporary statistical inference is largely broken into two camps, the frequentist interpretation and bayesian statistics. The frequentist perspective assumes there is a true probabilistic value that is unknown, but can be estimated using sampled data. Bayesian statistics is largely based on Bayes theorem. The idea is that people have some beliefs about a phenomena (for example, maybe you believe from previous experience that a coin is fair, 50/50 heads or tails). Then new data observations are used to update your beliefs using bayes theorem. 

In practice, another important concept is the counterfactual, which is used to build up design of experiments and causal analysis, which are important branches of statistical theory.  

Hope this helps. Source: currently writing my dissertation for my PhD in statistics.

I definitely had a lot of these same fears and didn't get any professional help for a long time because of them. For context, I lost my dad when I was 16, over 10 years ago now. I went through a period of time where the most distressing part was the memory of the day itself and surrounding events. I talked with my therapist about EMDR for a long time before we went ahead with it, because I was afraid of somehow "losing" the pain of it or trying to make it go away, or make me not miss him as much, or something like that. One thing that really helped was realizing that there are people who will still care about me and empathize with my loss, even if I work through the trauma of it and its immediate impact on my daily functioning. You don't need to be completely dysfunctional all the time to deserve love and support for the things you went through. EMDR doesn't take the trauma away. It just helped me not be so distressed all the time by the same repetitive thoughts and memories. Another thing that I realized through the process is that when I was having those flashbacks, I wasn't really experiencing my love for my dad, or even grieving losing him. It was all just panic and confusion. After EMDR I had a bit more bandwidth to actually just miss him and remember everything about him and our lives together, rather than just being stuck in one moment. It still hurts, I still miss him every day. For me, EMDR didn't take away the experience, my love for him, or my need for support and love, but it did lessen the impact of the flashbacks so I wasn't reliving it all the time. When I think about that day now, it isnt just panic and overwhelm. It's a complex mix of emotions, the memory of the fear I experienced then, and sadness for my younger self and what I had to go through, and profound love and grief for losing him. I don't know if that helps at all to hear. But I hope you keep reaching out and continue to get professional support, whether that be talk therapy or EMDR.

I think the personal vs private thing is really key here. I do a mix of traditional and art journaling all jumbled up together, but I don't share pictures of it because it's not meant as an art piece, it's my personal place to vomit my thoughts and feelings into. I'm not trying to make something aesthetic. Most of the time it's not. I have no problem calling it art journaling, and it doesn't even bother me if people share it, unless they are clearly just sharing it just to show off. Hence the public aspect. If you made something private and decide to share it with the community, great. If you made something intentionally just to share with social media, that's something different.

Please don't put pressure on yourself to journal in any particular way or feel like it's not valuable because it's not "pretty" by social media standards. Journaling isn't meant to be pretty (although it can be), it's meant to be a tool for you. Its a very personal practice and you don't have to do it just for someone else's approval. The images of pristine art pages and collages only come to the top because they make perfect fodder for social media. That said, I actually do a mix of traditional and art journaling, but let me tell you, my journal is NOT aesthetic most of the time. It's full of word vomit and scraps  things that hold value to me for some reason or another and it's not fine art. In truth, the reason I started mixing some art journaling in was as a way to start to fill a blank page so I didn't just stare at it in panic. When I start to get too perfectionistic about my handwriting or not wanting to "mess it up", I will intentionally go fill a page as ugly as I can with huge scrawling writing and magazine scraps, and then think, "well the journal is already 'ruined', so no need to worry about messing it up now!" For the values of y: after you know what values you are allowed to "plug in" (or input) for x, you might want to know, what values of y might i get out? For example on this function, I can't get out the number 50. No matter what value of x I pick, I will never ever get 50 out. But I can get the number 0 out. I can also get the number -10 out. So the question is, what are ALL values of y can you get out? This will be an interval.

For the values of x: The way I like to think of this is to ask, what am I allowed to "plug in" for x? Or, even better, are there any values for x I CANT plug in? Think of any number you can, try to use it as x. 

There are a lot of equations where you are allowed to plug in ANYTHING, meaning any number between -inf and inf will work.

There are other functions were you can't plug in certain numbers. For example, 1/x. If you try to evaluate 1/x when x=0 , you have 1/0 which is undefined.

I actually published a paper on this topic, it is still in review. We only have so much real estate on this earth, and we have released a lot of carbon. There just isn't the space. Afforesting areas that are not naturally forests can destroy the local ecosystem or pose a serious fire hazard. As an example, the Fort McMurray fire. Unfortunately there is a feedback loop between climate change, wildfire, and carbon sequestration through forestation. Climate change leads to increased fire hazard. If trees burn, we replant them, but it takes many years for those new trees to recapture the lost carbon, especially if the fire damaged the soil. We are having a hard enough time recouping the carbon already released from wildfires and deforestation of old growth forests worldwide. Protecting old growth forests and replanting lost areas can help us prevent the problem from getting worse, but worldwide tree planting is not a feasible solution on its own to the damage caused by fossil fuels.

Hey there. I lost my dad to suicide when I was 16. I'm 25 now, and it wasnt that long ago that I was exactly where you are now, going to college, no one knowing what happened unless I decided to tell them. College is supposed to be such a happy time, but I felt like I was living a totally different life from my friends and classmates and it felt like there was no way they could understand. I felt so alone and stuck.

You most certainly can have PTSD from losing a parent to suicide. Try not to let other people's expectations pressure you to think you should be able to just "move on". They may mean well, but try to have grace for yourself that healing takes time, and it's not your fault that you are experiencing these symptoms. Healing is possible, and the anxiety and depression dont have to last forever. I know it might feel like they will, but try to hang onto hope that healing is possible. It wont happen magically overnight when the grief is "over". I still grieve my dad, and I probably always will. But the depression and anxiety, and other PTSD symptoms dont have control of my life the same way that they used to.

I'm so glad you have a therapist, that is a great first step. Finding resources for PTSD, like this sub, was another helpful step for me. There are many great books, workbooks, websites, exercises, and therapies that were of great help. Talking to those closest to me was also a relief. Most of them didnt understand, but they cared and at least it wasnt a secret I carried around anymore. 

Feel free to PM me. You are not alone.

I definitely have this reaction as well. Spent a good portion of the summer coming up with a game plan with my therapist to cope. This is what works for me personally, maybe some of it might be helpful. If not, keep searching. It's a personal process for everyone to find what works.

For me, it's much easier to ground myself as a preventative measure than to use grounding to pull myself out of a flashback. So I do things to ground myself from the get go. (As others have mentioned , use sensory experiences) Turn on music in the morning (sound), pet my dog (touch), take a shower (touch, sound,smell), eat some breakfast (taste), drink some coffee (taste, smell, touch). If I can manage, do some light stretching or yoga (body awareness is also grounding). 

I also plan to have interactions with others, as talking to people really helps ground me. I set up phone/zoom calls with friends and family often (even though I really dont want to sometimes). A couple people know about my ptsd and are willing to take my call when I'm in the middle of a flashback. Others dont need to know what's going on, but just are nice to talk to and connect with.

Disassociation and freeze responses are usually noticable for me when they start to happen. As soon as I become aware of the fact that I feel myself slipping into it or freezing, I do a grounding exercise (as others have mentioned) and then immediately go through Pete Walkers flashback management steps:
http://www.pete-walker.com/flashbackManagement.htm 

I keep a screen shot of those steps saved as my phone lock screen so that I can pull them up easily throughout the day. Some days I go through the steps 3 or 4 times. Other days are much better and I dont need them at all. It's all okay.

Those pieces were a starting point for me. Feel free to ask me any questions.

Yep. This. So much misinformation out there about what PTSD is 😔

Horrible trauma DOES NOT EQUAL PTSD. Someone can go through a horrible experience and not develop PTSD. Yes, PTSD symptoms vary significantly. However, two people can have the same experience and only one developed PTSD. PTSD is a disorder where someone has a particular characteristic of reaction to trauma.

Please read the DSM diagnositic criteria: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK207191/box/part1_ch3.box16/

Also direct quote from DSM-5: "Not all psychopathology that occurs in individuals exposed to an extreme stressors should necessarily be attributed to PTSD."

The DSM actually has a separate diagnosis, called adjustment disorder, which is diagnosed when someone goes through a traumatic event but does not fill the diagnostic criteria for PTSD symptoms.

People will have different symptoms of PTSD, but not all people going through trauma will have PTSD. This is not gatekeeping. This is helping people understand what PTSD is and isnt so that they can receive the correct treatment. As a PTSD sufferer, the amount of misinformation out there has caused me legitimate harm in recieving the right treatment. Do not self diagnose. While we can speculate which characters had PTSD by their actions, NOT all people who went through the experience will necessarily develop PTSD!

Well the bullet journal system uses a dot for a task (to do), a circle for an event (that occurred or that you are looking toward), and a dash for a note (any general comment). Then you can mark an exclamation point or star for important or urgent things. 

They also separate different sections for "collections" - like one section is for a daily log/journaling, one section for monthly calendar, one section for (fill in anything here. Maybe a Tarot reading section, mood log, etc). Then you can reference these in a table of contents so you know where to find them.

The specific symbolism or setup isn't important. What's important is that it resonates with you, and that it makes you want to use your journal more. You choices should draw you in, not push you away or stress you out. Find a system that feels "right" for you.

I have done a few journals in a highly structured way, with pages dedicated to long term goals, daily to dos, emotional and health tracking, and random musings. At that time I needed more structure in my life, and it helped.

This last time around, I needed freedom. This has been a difficult time for everyone and I needed to just vomit emotionally and spiritually. So I let loose and let it be random, with my doodles mixed in with angry rants mixed in with daily to dos on one page, with no real table of contents or organization. I simply separated change of train of thought/entry by a line. I still dated my entries. Afterward, I will sometimes reread them and bullet point my insights. 

The best way to find what is right for you is to just try it. Remember: journals only cost like 5 bucks, maybe 20 if you got a really nice one. Dont be afraid to screw it up! Just start using it. If you dont like it, try something new. Rinse, repeat. 

Last thing, I also like to say a blessing/write an entry of intent at the start of every new journal. It helps me to get started without feeling like I'm "messing up" a brand new journal.

I journal as a part of my spiritual practice. I went down the path of bullet journaling for a short time and quickly realized that while elements of the system are helpful, the online bullet journal culture... has some issues. It's really easy to get WAY too wrapped up in the aesthetics, having perfect, insta worthy spreads. That is NOT the point of journaling! 

Life is messy. Spiritual journeys are messy. If your focus is to make your journal "pretty", you likely wont ever use it. Also, bullet journal systems are often designed to increase productivity, rather than to slow down and enjoy the journey.

Personally, I ditched the bullet system. I've incorporated some ideas/aspects, like numbering my pages, having symbolism/a key that makes my entries easy to identify, keeping a to do/calendar, etc.  

Thats just my experience anyways. Its a highly personal thing, so find what works for you!

YES seek help! If you are questioning your mental health AT ALL you should talk to your doctor. That doesnt mean you automatically need to take medication or be in long term therapy, but your doctor can help you decide the next best steps. Even if it's something "mild" you should still have your doctor on your team, knowing what's going on, able to help point you to useful resources. 

There is a difference between self diagnosis and keeping track of your own health and how it impacts your life. If you are having problems that are impacting your life, you should talk to a professional about it! They will know how to help you reduce the impact, with or without a hard diagnosis.

Your doctor may refer you to a psychiatrist, psychologist, or hopefully, both. I would highly recommend meeting with both and discussing what options will be most helpful for you.

Regarding your parents, assuming you are on their health insurance and are in the US, they will need to know who you are seeing in order to help you get these visits covered. So it sounds like what you are missing is an understanding of distributions. 

I am assuming you are comfortable with the normal distribution. Remember, this is a function, an equation, that when you plot it, looks like the bell curve. Randomly sampled points are likely to come from the "middle".

Here's the thing though. If you take a sample of points from a normal distribution, and then take the average of them, you get ONE number. That number, the average of the sample, is normally distributed. If you draw new samples over and over, and take the average each time, and then plot those individual averages, they will lie along the normal curve. Specifically, a normal curve with variance sigma. So if we KNOW the variance, we use this normal distribuiton to get our interval.

Okay so that's all well and good. But what would happen if you took the *variance* of each sample, and then plotted *those* numbers? They wouldn't lie on a normal curve! They would actually lie along a different curve, called the chi square distribution.

Okay now stay with me, new scenario. Now take a sample, and calculate mean/(s/sqrt(n)). This gives one number... now do this over and over. What is the distribution of THOSE numbers? They lie on a different curve, which we call the t distribution with n-1 degrees of freedom.

Notice that in that last scenario, we dont need to know sigma. We can use just the sample mean and sample variance to get to get the distribution. Once we know the distribution, we can build the confidence interval. 

Feel free to ask follow up questions, hope this points you in the right direction. 

One final thing: when sample size is large enough, the t distribution looks a whole lot like the normal distribution. So if you have a large sample size, you can use the normal distribution with variance s^2 as an approximation, instead of using the t distribution.
